intro: In a distant future, when the world is at a dead end because of pollution,the artificial intelligence systems start a planet defense protocol.
The biggest AI system, EKKO, turns against humanity, claiming that you are the cause of environmental deterioration,lacking circular thinking about economy and pollution.
The famous scientist Helsink makes a plan to help you infiltrate in EKKO’s building.
He builds a small robot named C1-rcle through which you can enter EKKO’s building without being detected.
Pay attention to the clues left throughout the journey and you will surely manage to pass the levels inside the building and prove to the AI that humans can also have “circular” thinking.

book.title: The Experts’ Manual in Circular Economy

pages.title: I. Linear vs. Circular Economic Model
pages.content:
The modern economy has functioned for a long time on a linear model, based on the idea that resources are numerous and cheap. This model assumes the following process: raw materials are extracted, goods are produced from them, the goods are consumed, and then they are thrown away. Often, this approach leads to the depletion of resources, accumulation of waste and environmental pollution.

Thus, the circular economy appears as an alternative, which proposes extending the lifespan of products, reducing the consumption of new resources, and also eliminating the notion of 'final waste'. Instead of products becoming useless, they are repaired, reused or transformed into other products.

pages.title: II. The Idea of 'Closed Loop'
pages.content:
A central principle of the circular economy is closing the material cycle. This means that materials do not leave the economic system, but circulate continuously between uses.

There are two types of cycles:
  - Biological: materials return back to nature (e.g. compost)
  - Technical: materials are reused in the industrial process.

A very important concept is waste valorization, which involves transforming waste into useful resources (e.g. food leftovers become compost; plastic becomes raw material for other products, etc.)

pages.title: III. How the Circular Economy Creates Value
pages.content:
The concept of circular economy does not refer only to environmental protection, but also to creating economic value. It operates at:
  - Macro level: policies and national economies
  - Meso level: industries and supply chains
  - Micro level: companies and consumers

Among the advantages of the circular economy are: cost reduction (because fewer raw materials are used), creation of new markets and innovation. Also, the energy used tends to be renewable, and resources are used much more efficiently.

pages.title: IV. Sustainable Development (SDGs)
pages.content: The United Nations created 17 global objectives for a more sustainable future. The circular economy contributes to these objectives by reducing waste, lowering pollution, and using resources efficiently. It also supports economic growth, fosters innovation and contributes to more sustainable cities.

pages.title: V. Practical Examples
pages.content:
Examples of circular economy applications in the world:
  - Cities implementing recycling and compost systems
  - 'Zero waste' programs that significantly reduce the amount of waste

These initiatives include:
  - Infrastructure for recycling
  - Education for citizens
  - Public policies

pages.title: VI. European Policies
pages.content:
The European Commission promotes the circular economy through concrete policies. These policies aim at:
  - Durable products from the design phase
  - Transparency towards consumers
  - Reducing industrial impact

Thus, emphasis is placed on durability, reparability and recyclability.

pages.title: VII. Circular Business Models
pages.content:
The circular economy also changes how companies operate. There are several strategies such as:
  - Transforming the existing model
  - Creating new businesses
  - Expanding activities
  - Integrating already existing circular models

Also, service-based models appear (e.g. renting instead of buying), and companies begin to retain responsibility over products.

pages.title: VIII. Bioeconomy and Its Applications
pages.content:
Bioeconomy is based on the use of biological resources (plants, animals, microorganisms) to create food, energy, materials or even industrial products. It replaces fossil resources, supports sustainability and contributes to reducing emissions.

Bioeconomy has diverse applications in several fields:

ENVIRONMENT:
  - Soil cleaning (also called bioremediation)
  - Pollution reduction

MEDICINE:
  - Vaccines
  - Genetic therapies

INDUSTRY:
  - Bioplastics
  - Biofuels

AGRICULTURE:
  - Resistant crops
  - Biological fertilizers

pages.title: IX. Circular Bioeconomy
pages.content: The concept of circular bioeconomy combines the efficiency of the circular economy with the resources provided by bioeconomy. It focuses on biomass use, reducing biological waste and optimizing the use of available resources.

pages.title: X. The 'Cascading' Principle
pages.content:
The cascading principle refers to using a resource multiple times, not just once, so biomass can be used in several successive stages.

For example:
  - Wood => furniture
  - Furniture => recycled materials
  - Materials => energy

Thus, the value of the resource is maximized and waste is reduced.

pages.title: XI. Biorefinery
pages.content: A biorefinery is a facility that transforms biomass into useful products and produces energy and materials at the same time. Products may include fuels, materials or chemical substances.

pages.title: XII. European Green Deal
pages.content:
The European Green Deal is the European Union's strategy to transform the current economy into a sustainable one. This includes clean energy, green industry, sustainable mobility and sustainable agriculture.

The objective of this plan is to achieve climate neutrality by 2050.

pages.title: XIII. Equity and Society
pages.content:
The transition to a circular economy must be fair and inclusive, providing support for vulnerable groups, equal access to opportunities, as well as education and training.

Sustainability is not only about nature, but also about people.
